topic: OJCP: An Open Protocol for Agent-Consumable Job Data
research_method: curl/urllib primary-source retrieval (spec, site, GitHub raw + gh CLI API, HN Algolia API, launch PR). No browser rendering used. Secondhand industry figures are labeled as such.
summary: OJCP (Open Job Context Protocol) is a draft v0.2 open standard, authored by Austin Anderson (CTO, Recruitics) and governed by a nine-seat steering committee (Workday, CrossCountry Healthcare, Recruitics, LoopCV, Hiring.cafe, aiApply, scale.jobs, Tink, plus invited expert Andrew Nolan, WebMCP co-creator). It is not a competing protocol: it is a vertical application of MCP for the job domain. Providers expose /.well-known/ojcp.json, implement at least the search_jobs tool (six standard tools total), and declare a normalized apply-path taxonomy; agents that already speak MCP can call OJCP directly. 7 schemas, verifiable agent identity via HTTP Message Signatures / Web Bot Auth, manifest signing with JWKS, and PII-free identity verification proofs (ID.me, Clear) round out the trust model. Status is early: 80 stars on GitHub, 3 implementing organizations listed in ADOPTERS.md, reference provider live at ojcp.dev, conformance suite reporting 10/10 passing against that provider.

sibling_repos.purpose: Conformance test suite (@ojcp/conformance): validates a provider's manifest, job postings and MCP tool responses; CLI + programmatic API
Provider registry — one reviewed JSON entry per provider, added by PR; domain control proven per README; surfaces as registry.ojcp.dev with an MCP tool find_ojcp_providers

product_facts.versioning: Draft v0.2 (CHANGELOG entry dated 2026-09-22). Schema $id namespace stays at /v0.1/; ojcp_version accepts both '0.1' and '0.2' so existing providers keep validating — v0.2 changes are additive/backward-compatible.
product_facts.licensing: Dual-licensed by content type: specification/schemas/examples/docs = CC BY 4.0; code/tooling/CI = Apache License 2.0. Spec text also carries an Apache-2.0 notice.
product_facts.governance: Nine-seat founding steering committee, each holding one seat and no veto. Members: Austin Anderson (Recruitics, spec author), Hamed Nilforoshan (Hiring.cafe), Bryan Hughes (CrossCountry Healthcare), David Stevens (Workday), Peter Utekal (aiApply), Balaji Kummari (scale.jobs), Tom Chevalier (Tink), Lucas Simopoulos (LoopCV), Andrew Nolan (WebMCP co-creator, invited-expert seat). Diversity constraint: no more than two seats per market segment; odd-number requirement; eleven-seat cap.
product_facts.bootstrap_rule: Until 5 of 9 seats are filled by ratified appointees, all spec-affecting decisions require a public RFC with a minimum 30-day comment window plus documented rationale in docs/decisions/.
product_facts.custom_tools: Provider-specific tools MUST use namespaced names {provider}:{tool_name} (e.g. acme:get_referral_link, greenhouse:schedule_interview); standard tools use bare names and agents MUST recognize them. Custom tools self-describe via MCP tools/list.

apply_paths.desc: Apply directly via ATS (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, etc.)
Provider controls the apply flow and delivers to ATS
Third-party platform owns the flow (e.g. Indeed Apply, Easy Apply)

product_facts.spec_sections: 18 sections: Introduction/Terminology, Job Manifest, Job Tools, Data Schemas, Apply Paths, Resume Upload, Provider Trust (threat model, manifest signing, JWK set discovery + key rotation, validation procedure, registry trust tiers unverified/verified/audited, agent obligations), Agent Identity (signing profile, key discovery, identity binding, personal-agent delegation), Identity Verification (two delivery models, proof format, async polling, abandonment), WebMCP Integration, Feed Discovery, Security and Privacy, Interoperability, Versioning, Conformance, IANA Considerations, Open Questions, Acknowledgements
product_facts.identity_stack: HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) on the Web Bot Auth wire profile; Ed25519 recommended; agent publishes keys at a signatures directory and names its key via the Signature-Agent header; providers declare support under auth.agent_signatures. A verified identity is a hint about the agent, not proof a human authorized the action — that needs an optional user-rooted user_mandate on the AgentDeclaration.
product_facts.verification_proofs: JWS/JWE proof delivered by a third-party Identity Verifier (ID.me, Clear). Required claims: iss, aud, sub, iat, exp, nonce; nonce is set to the application_id to prevent replay; subject_hash (SHA-256) instead of PII. Two delivery models: agent_submitted (verifier returns proof to the agent, agent includes it in submit_application) and provider_managed (verifier delivers proof straight to the provider via callback/iframe postMessage; agent must NOT include proofs).
product_facts.reference_provider: https://ojcp.dev is a live OJCP provider (dogfood endpoint). Manifest fetched from https://ojcp.dev/.well-known/ojcp.json declares mcp_endpoint https://ojcp.dev/api/mcp, tools search_jobs/get_job_detail/get_employer_context/begin_application/submit_application/check_application_status, apply_paths provider_hosted + ats_direct, auth type none ('This reference provider requires no authentication'), rate_limits anonymous_rps 10 / authenticated_rps 100.

evaluating: reqspace.ai — evaluating a provider manifest over customer career pages plus AgentDeclaration for its candidate-side auto-apply agent (2026-09)

Imperative API document.modelContext.registerTool() and declarative form annotations (toolname/tooldescription/toolparamdescription)

product_facts.get_started: Ship a manifest at /.well-known/ojcp.json (must be Content-Type: application/json), expose the standard tools over any MCP-compatible transport, then run the conformance suite (npx @ojcp/conformance validate manifest.json). Browser-native path: register tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() or annotate existing HTML apply forms with toolname/tooldescription so the browser translates them into tools.

key_points: The normative spec itself is the top-ranked result for the topic and the hardest act to follow — it is 18 sections of MUST/SHOULD language with JSON payloads.
Frames OJCP as a vertical of MCP: 'MCP defines how agents call tools; OJCP defines which tools exist for job search, application, and verification' — 'An agent that speaks MCP already speaks OJCP.'

Manifest MUST live at /.well-known/ojcp.json with Content-Type: application/json; MUST include ojcp_version, provider.name, tools; SHOULD include mcp_endpoint, feed_endpoints, apply_paths, auth, rate_limits, supported_verifiers; MAY include resume_upload and a manifest signature.
Only search_jobs is mandatory; the other five tools are RECOMMENDED. Custom tools must be namespaced {provider}:{tool}.

Naming convention split worth reproducing for readers: schema.org-origin fields stay camelCase (employmentType, experienceLevel, jobLocation, baseSalary); OJCP extension fields and tool params are snake_case (skills_required, team_context, urgency, salary_min); agents SHOULD handle both.

Provider Trust section defines threat model, manifest signing with JWKS discovery and key rotation, and three registry trust tiers (unverified / verified / audited) that drive agent obligations about transmitting PII.
§17 Open Questions is present in the table of contents — a useful honesty signal for a fair write-up.

Marketing surface: 'The open standard for agent-native job data', founding-member logos, and the pitch that OJCP is 'shaped by employers, ATS vendors, job boards, staffing agencies, and agent platforms — each holding one seat, none holding a veto.'

Value bullets an article must answer or beat: MCP-native tools, structured discovery via a well-known manifest, normalized apply paths, consent-first privacy (resume embeddings for fit scoring without transmitting PII), agent-aware ranking returning fit_score and fit_rationale, and WebMCP readiness.
Publishes the apply-path taxonomy as a table with per-type agent-submission support — the clearest single artefact for explaining the standard visually.
The site itself is the live reference provider (playground calls hit the same endpoint MCP clients use), which makes 'try it now' sections easy to write and hard for a text-only competitor to match.
README ranks highly and carries the project's own framing plus the repository layout, so a guide should link deep into /spec, /schemas, /examples and /docs/decisions rather than paraphrase them.

Ships explicit project status: everything under 'Shipped' (v0.2 draft + schemas, reference provider, nine-seat committee, verifiable agent identity, canonical official_job_url trust anchor, conformance suite + registry, first independent provider FoundRole) and 'In progress' (action-bound user mandates and the consent/authorization flow, growing the registry and adopter set).
States the interoperability table plainly — MCP, WebMCP, HTTP Message Signatures/Web Bot Auth, schema.org/JobPosting, Indeed/Zip XML feeds via adapter.
Contribution path is documented: RFCs in docs/rfcs/, DCO sign-off, conformance validation, ADOPTERS.md listing.

The vendor-side narrative to correct or corroborate: 'AI agents... flooding HR inboxes', 'most of those submissions are low-quality, mismatched, or contain false candidate information, because the AI agents have no reliable way to assess fit before applying' — which is precisely the gap OJCP's structured job data and fit scoring target.

Quantified industry claims (estimates, not primary research): 70% of job seekers use AI tools; AI bots generate more web traffic than humans; large employers see nearly one-third of inbound applications from AI agents.
Quote usable for a pull-quote: Adam Stafford (Recruitics CEO) — 'Within the next two years, AI-enabled job applications will make up the vast majority of open positions posted publicly.'
Positions the standard as the fix for the AI application crisis rather than as a technical protocol — the editorial hook most competing articles will borrow.

The author's own summary is the best one-paragraph explanation available: 'OJCP is MCP tools for search and apply, a manifest at /.well-known/ojcp.json so agents can find providers, and schemas that extend schema.org instead of replacing it.'

The strongest technical argument in the thread — 'Inference can't produce authorization... a more capable agent is also a more capable impersonator' — is the reason the trust sections exist and is worth building the article's thesis around.
Real-world status detail a reader cares about: the author says OJCP 'might soon be implemented into https://github.com/dakheera47/Job-Ops', i.e. consumer tooling is only indirectly available today.

Fair criticism to include: a commenter objects to the word 'protocol' this early, says no committee members were visible other than Recruitics, and points readers at GOVERNANCE.md and Discussions to check. GOVERNANCE.md now lists all nine holders, so the criticism is partly answered by the current repo state.
Also raised in-thread: ghosting/blacklisting of companies that ignore applicants, and whether headless hiring eventually makes recruiters optional — both are good FAQ material.

The clearest alternative standard in the same lane: Open Job Protocol (OJP) v0.2, MIT licensed, 'machine-first, vendor-neutral JSON standard for job opportunities' with flat snake_case top-level fields and strict additionalProperties: false.

A valid OJP document needs 10 required top-level fields (schema_version, ojp_id, created_at, updated_at, status, title, description, employment_type, organization, location); salary, requirements, team and process are optional; salary_transparency is employer-controlled.

Bilateral design: OJP covers the employer/job half and its companion Open Talent Protocol (OTP) v0.2 (opentalentprotocol.org) covers the candidate/profile half with progressive disclosure tiers so most agent traffic can run on cheaper models.
Explicitly positioned against schema.org: 'schema.org/JobPosting serves Google, not hiring agents' — and it ships a validator CLI plus migration guides from v0.1.

Neutral framing for the article: OJP/OTP is a JSON document standard, OJCP is an MCP tool + discovery + trust standard; neither is a superset of the other, and no cross-standard adapter is documented yet.

The conformance suite is the practical verification stop a guide should end with: npx @ojcp/conformance validate manifest.json (or --type job-posting), plus a runConformanceSuite() call against a live domain.

Documents exactly what a provider must produce to pass: valid manifest, ojcp_version present, tools array present, search_jobs listed, mcp_endpoint declared, MCP endpoint answering initialize, search_jobs returning a jobs array, first job validating against the JobPosting schema, get_job_detail returning a job, begin_application returning a session.
Publishes a reproducible pass/fail baseline for the reference provider (10 passed, 0 failed, 8 jobs returned) that a reader can re-run against their own implementation.

competitors.source: Official site / reference provider (authored by Recruitics)
key_points: Positioning: 'the open standard for agent-native job data', built on MCP, interoperable with schema.org, governed by an independent steering committee.
Discovery: providers expose a manifest at /.well-known/ojcp.json declaring tools, mcp_endpoint, apply_paths, auth, rate_limits.

Six standard MCP tools: search_jobs (required), get_job_detail, get_employer_context, begin_application, submit_application, check_application_status; custom tools use namespaced names such as acme:get_referral_link.

Seven core schemas: manifest.json, job-posting.json (extends schema.org/JobPosting), candidate-context.json, agent-declaration.json, verification-step.json, verification-proof.json, verifier-manifest.json.
Apply-path taxonomy: ats_direct, provider_hosted, platform_native, email, external_redirect, custom - each declaring whether agent submission is supported.
Consent-first privacy: resume embeddings enable fit scoring without transmitting PII; agents self-declare identity.
WebMCP-ready via document.modelContext; a live playground at /api/mcp serves mock data; the /registry page currently exposes only a domain-validation form, no provider list.
Internal inconsistency worth flagging: the home page says an independent steering committee, the governance page says 9 seats, and the same site footer says 'Recruitics holds one seat of seven'.

competitors.source: Official specification (living document; renders as version 0.2)
key_points: 18 sections: manifest, tools, data schemas, apply paths, resume upload, provider trust, agent identity, identity verification, WebMCP, feed discovery, security/privacy, interoperability, versioning, conformance, IANA considerations, open questions.

Versioning: CHANGELOG shows 0.1 (2026-03-06) then 0.2 (2026-09-22); changes are additive, the schema $id namespace stays at /v0.1/ and ojcp_version accepts both '0.1' and '0.2' so existing providers keep validating.

Concrete freshness rules an implementer must code to: re-fetch manifests at most hourly (Cache-Control max-age=3600); search results MUST NOT be cached for more than 15 minutes (max-age=900); get_job_detail may be cached up to 1 hour; application session tokens have a RECOMMENDED 30-minute TTL and must never be reused.
Rate limiting: HTTP 429 with Retry-After on REST, JSON-RPC error -32029 with retry_after_seconds on MCP; agents must not retry before the window and should use exponential backoff with jitter.

Consent scopes gate fields: search_personalization (skills, experience_years, location/employment preference) -> fit_scoring (current_title, salary_expectation, work_authorization, resume_embedding_hash) -> application_prefill (name, email, resume_url) -> full_profile. Providers MUST drop out-of-scope fields rather than reject the request and SHOULD emit a warning.

Registry trust tiers: unverified (manifest parses), verified (signed manifest plus confirmed employer identity), audited (passes conformance suite, security review, and 90 days with no abuse reports). Agents MUST cap consent_scope for weak-trust providers and MAY filter with min_trust_tier.

Identity verification without PII: JWS VerificationProof with required claims iss/aud/sub/iat/exp/nonce; algorithms ES256 (recommended), RS256, ES384, RS384; subject_hash is SHA-256 of a canonical subject identifier and must not be reversible; verifiers publish keys at /.well-known/ojcp-verifier.json with signing_algorithms and public_keys_url (JWKS).

Agent identity (section 8, RFC 0001): verifiable agent_id using RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures on the Web Bot Auth wire profile - JWKS directory, Signature-Agent header, Ed25519, PSL-based origin binding. A verified identity is a hint about the agent, not proof a human authorized the action; that is what user_mandate is for.

Feed discovery: the well-known manifest plus an OJCP Registry exposing the MCP tool find_ojcp_providers (filters: industry, employer_name, location, has_agent_apply, min_trust_tier). Registry governance is listed as an open question and registry.ojcp.dev does not resolve yet.

IANA: registers two well-known URIs (ojcp.json, ojcp-verifier.json) per RFC 8615, to be submitted once the spec reaches stable status; it consumes /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory from Web Bot Auth.

Open questions the spec admits: form_skill_url companion schema, whether CandidateContext becomes its own RFC, registry governance, verifier internal protocol, and whether user_mandate gets standardized (RFC 0003 action-bound user mandates is in progress).

competitors.source: HR Tech Feed, 2026-07-30 (trade coverage of the 2026-07-29 EINPresswire launch release)
key_points: Launch framing: Recruitics announced OJCP with a coalition including Workday, Cross Country Healthcare, HiringCafe, AIApply, scale.jobs and LoopCV; Recruitics CTO Austin Anderson authored the spec.

Quoted industry numbers: about 70% of job seekers already use AI in the job search; AI bots generate more web traffic than humans; large employers see nearly one-third of inbound applications coming from AI agents, largely low-quality or mismatched.
Adam Stafford (CEO, Recruitics): 'Within the next two years, AI-enabled job applications will make up the vast majority of open positions posted publicly.'
Andrew Nolan (WebMCP co-creator): 'I see OJCP as a promising application of the agentic web for hiring.'
Stated goal: reduce application noise, protect candidate data, and give employers structured fit signals and verification requirements before a submission happens.
Caveat: the 70% and one-third figures are 'industry estimates' with no primary study cited - attribute them to Recruitics, do not assert them as measured.

competitors.source: Open Job Protocol (OJP) v0.2 - the rival standard worth comparing against
key_points: A different, simpler approach: a machine-first, vendor-neutral JSON document schema rather than an MCP tool surface. MIT licensed, with no required registry, platform, or ATS.

v0.2 requires only 10 top-level fields (schema_version, ojp_id, created_at, updated_at, status, title, description, employment_type, organization, location); flat snake_case keys with strict additionalProperties: false for reliable parsing.
Positions schema.org/JobPosting as serving Google rather than hiring agents; uses the ESCO taxonomy for skills and a must_have / nice_to_have split agents can filter and rank on.
Pairs with the Open Talent Protocol (OTP) for the candidate side - bilateral matching, mirroring OJCP's provider/agent split.

Interoperability by mapping: 'Mappable to schema.org/JobPosting, Google for Jobs, LinkedIn Job Posting API, and HR-XML', with a validator CLI and a v0.1 to v0.2 migration guide (neogene-ai/open-job-protocol).

Use in the post: OJCP is a protocol (tools, discovery, trust, verification); OJP is a data format. They overlap only on 'structured job posting for agents', and neither has meaningful adoption yet - compare scope, not winners.

Hacker News reception was modest and skeptical: the Show HN ran twice (2026-08-11: 11 points / 2 comments; 2026-08-12: 39 points / 10 comments). Main criticisms: the word 'protocol' is diluted by an early single-vendor effort, and reviewers could not find the other committee members listed publicly.

Name collision hazard: 'OJCP' also means Ontario Job Creation Partnerships (Government of Ontario, eopg.labour.gov.on.ca), which competes for the acronym in search results - disambiguate in the title or intro.

angles: Lead with the author's own thesis: 'Inference can't produce authorization.' An agent can work out what a form wants, but it cannot establish that a specific human consented to this specific submission — so the protocol's real product is trust, not JSON. This separates the article from every 'here is another manifest format' write-up.

Explain OJCP as a vertical of MCP rather than a rival: 'MCP defines how agents call tools; OJCP defines which tools exist for job search, application and verification.' An agent that already speaks MCP speaks OJCP — you only need to discover the manifest. This lowers the perceived integration cost and is the strongest adoption argument in the docs.

The pain it removes is concrete and quotable: today's applying agents scrape career pages and 'fight ATS forms with Playwright/Browser Use, which breaks constantly (or they get bot blocked)' — career-page scraping is brittle by design, and a well-known manifest plus six typed tools replaces it.

Do the honest traction audit the marketing does not: 80 GitHub stars, 3 implementing organizations, 0-star registry repo, a stale 52-star badge, and ADOPTERS.md still showing unfilled steering seats next to GOVERNANCE.md's named holders. Early-stage standard with real corporate names attached — say both halves.

Surface the governance tension the HN thread raised and the repo later addressed: the committee was founded at seven seats and is seated at nine during a bootstrap period, and all spec-affecting decisions need a 30-day public RFC until 5 of 9 seats are ratified. That is unusually strict for a vendor-led standard and worth crediting.

Explain the consent and privacy architecture properly, because it is genuinely novel: CandidateContext is consent-scoped, resume_embedding_hash enables fit scoring without transmitting resume text, and identity verification returns a signed JWS proof containing only a subject_hash (SHA-256) plus timestamps — no PII flows through the protocol.
Call out nonce = application_id as replay protection and the two proof-delivery modes (agent_submitted vs provider_managed) as the decision point that actually changes an implementer's architecture.

Give the WebMCP on-ramp its own section: annotate existing apply forms with toolname/tooldescription instead of deploying a separate MCP server, and detect agent submissions via SubmitEvent.agentInvoked. This is the cheapest path for a mid-size employer and almost nobody writes it up.

Name the fork risk: Open Job Protocol (OJP) v0.2 plus Open Talent Protocol (OTP) on the candidate side is a second, unrelated JSON standard in the same lane, MIT licensed and also claiming to be agent-first. Two standards for one problem is the adoption story to watch, and no cross-standard adapter is documented yet.

Practical for job seekers: the standard's check_application_status tool is an API for status polling, which reframes ghosting from a cultural complaint into a data-availability problem — you can only be ghosted by a system that will not answer, and this makes answering a schema requirement.

Implementation walkthrough that doubles as SEO depth: write /.well-known/ojcp.json, satisfy the seven MUST/SHOULD/MAY manifest fields, implement search_jobs first, then run npx @ojcp/conformance validate and reproduce the 10-test baseline the reference provider passes.

Naming-convention gotcha as a genuine gotcha: schema.org-inherited fields stay camelCase while OJCP extensions and tool parameters are snake_case, and agents SHOULD handle both — the kind of detail that only appears if you actually read §4.1.

Draft-first honesty: call it what the repo calls it - a living draft v0.2 - and lead with the adoption reality (1 seated member, 2 small read-only providers, 1 evaluator) instead of the coalition press release. Nobody else reporting on OJCP has published that the reference provider fails its own 8/10 conformance run.

'It's not a new protocol, it's a vertical of MCP': the technical insight is that OJCP adds zero transport - an MCP client that can call tools already speaks OJCP, it just needs to fetch /.well-known/ojcp.json. Pair this with WebMCP so browser agents can hit the same tools with no server at all.

The consent-scope ladder is the part engineers should steal even if they never adopt OJCP: search_personalization -> fit_scoring -> application_prefill -> full_profile, where providers drop out-of-scope fields instead of rejecting requests, plus resume_embedding_hash for fit scoring without transmitting PII.

Trust is a runtime input to agent behaviour, not a badge: the spec tells agents to cap consent scope by registry tier and to withhold submission entirely for unsigned/unlisted providers. Trust tiers (unverified / verified / audited) and signed manifests are where the security story lives.

Show the working code path end to end (manifest probe -> search_jobs -> begin_application with AgentDeclaration -> submit/check status), including the freshness and rate-limit rules (15-minute search caching, 429 + Retry-After, JSON-RPC -32029, backoff with jitter). This is what makes it a guide rather than a news summary.

Verification without PII: the JWS VerificationProof (iss/aud/sub/iat/exp/nonce, ES256+, subject_hash = SHA-256, verifier JWKS at /.well-known/ojcp-verifier.json) is a reusable pattern for any agent protocol that must prove a human without shipping personal data.

Governance skepticism, cited not asserted: 9-seat committee vs six empty seats, the site's own 7-vs-9 seat contradiction, and the HN critique that the word 'protocol' is being diluted by a single-vendor early draft. Present the counter-evidence too (Recruitics says it is talking to OSS foundations; infra transfer is committed before v1.0).

OJCP vs OJP vs schema.org/JobPosting: three different layers (tool protocol, document schema, SEO markup). A decision matrix for 'what should I actually implement this quarter' is more useful than a feature table.

Disambiguation is a real SEO angle: OJCP is searched for the Ontario Job Creation Partnerships program; the post must own the 'ojcp job data protocol' / 'open job context protocol' phrasing explicitly in the title, first paragraph and FAQ.

What to do if you are an ATS or job board today: the cheapest first step is publishing /.well-known/ojcp.json with a search_jobs tool and letting the registry and conformance suite grade you - not a full apply-flow implementation.
